children: Prabodha Acharya underlined the need for companies to measure supply-chain footprints and focus decarbonisation efforts where commercial influence can deliver meaningful reductions

A company can measure emissions from its own operations, but its climate footprint rarely ends at the factory gate. Raw materials, suppliers, transportation and other parts of the value chain can add to emissions, leaving businesses with influence over sources they do not directly control.

That creates a difficult question for corporate climate commitments: where does accountability end when control runs out? Prabodha Acharya, Chief Sustainability Officer, JSW Group, distinguishes responsibility and accountability when it comes to Scope 3 emissions.
“You should be held accountable, not responsible,” Acharya said, arguing that businesses should know what is happening across their supply chains and use their influence to reduce emissions.
Accountability Without Control

Scope 3 emissions sit beyond a company’s direct operational boundaries, making their reduction dependent on suppliers and other value-chain partners. Companies have varying degrees of influence across supply-chain layers.

Acharya said companies should extend their influence to a reasonable point, depending on their size, purchasing power and relationship with suppliers. Influence can be stronger over Tier 1 suppliers but weaker across Tier 2 and Tier 3, making prioritisation important.

“Let us be pragmatic. Let us focus on what is material. What is important? What is really can change the needle? Focus on that,” he said, arguing that companies should concentrate resources where intervention can materially reduce emissions.
Measurement Comes First

Before reductions can be planned, companies need visibility over their supply-chain emissions. Yet data often sits outside the organisation, making measurement dependent on suppliers’ ability and willingness to disclose information.
Acharya rejected measurement difficulties as a reason to avoid Scope 3 accounting, pointing out that companies also faced challenges when systems for measuring direct emissions were evolving.
“Don't hide with the excuse that scope three is difficult to measure and monitor,” he said.

JSW has been evaluating suppliers for two to three years to understand its supply-chain footprint. Acharya said 80-90 per cent of suppliers disclosed their information. For JSW, Scope 3 emissions currently account for around 10-12 per cent of total emissions. The estimate could rise to 20-25 per cent if associated methane emissions from coal are included.
Smaller Suppliers, Bigger Constraints

The accountability question becomes more complicated when suppliers lack financial resources to decarbonise. MSMEs may have to choose between investing in emissions reduction and using limited capital for productivity or business improvements.

Acharya acknowledged this constraint, saying larger buyers can support smaller suppliers through training, awareness, and conditions. He also argued that businesses should prioritise major emission sources rather than apply identical expectations across suppliers.
This leaves a practical gap between what larger companies may seek from their supply chains and what smaller businesses can realistically deliver.

Companies in emissions-intensive industries must also reconcile production growth with decarbonisation. JSW Steel is doubling capacity while targeting a 42 per cent reduction in emission intensity by 2030, according to Acharya. It has achieved a 30 per cent reduction so far.
The company is also targeting an 18 million tonne reduction in emissions by 2030. The broader challenge remains whether reductions can keep pace with expanding production and demand.
From Responsibility To Influence

The distinction between responsibility and accountability puts influence at the centre of Scope 3 discussions. Companies may not control every emission in their value chains, but they can identify material sources, engage suppliers and use commercial relationships to encourage reductions.

This also makes decarbonisation a business decision, rather than only a reporting exercise. Acharya argued that companies need to consider environmental gains alongside commercial outcomes when making choices on sourcing, operations and suppliers. “Use sustainability to improve your competitiveness,” he said, suggesting that lower-emission alternatives can become more practical when they also make business sense.
The remarks came at the 9th Sustainable World Conclave 2026, during a discussion on corporate accountability for emissions beyond direct control.
